title: US Pressures Apple to Ditch Chinese Memory Chips Amid Global Shortage
excerpt: Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick told Apple to find alternatives to China for memory sourcing as AI-driven demand squeezes global supply chains.
body:
• US Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick told Apple to stop exploring Chinese memory chip makers CXMT and Yangtze Memory Technologies
  • A global memory shortage driven by AI data center demand is pushing prices higher, squeezing consumer electronics manufacturers
  • Apple is expanding iPhone assembly in India through contract manufacturing partners as part of broader supply chain diversification

The Trump administration has directly told Apple to find alternatives to China for memory chip sourcing, adding new friction to the iPhone maker's already complex supply chain at a time when a global memory shortage is driving up component costs.

US Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick said the administration "is not in favour" of Apple buying memory chips from Chinese manufacturers after touring an Apple manufacturing facility in Houston, according to a Wall Street Journal report.

"There have to be other solutions to the memory issue, but it's not great American companies using Chinese memory."

— Howard Lutnick, US Commerce Secretary

When asked whether he had communicated that position to Apple, Lutnick replied: "Plainly."

AI Boom Fuels the Memory Crunch

The confrontation comes as demand for memory chips has spiked sharply, driven in large part by companies building AI data centers. The resulting supply shortage has pushed prices higher, adding to costs across consumer electronics.

https://x.com/ResisttheMS/status/2088746221892698143

Apple has been testing memory chips from Chinese manufacturers CXMT and Yangtze Memory Technologies (YMTC), according to people familiar with the matter. Apple's chief operating officer Sabih Khan declined to confirm the testing but said that given the scale of the shortage, "we have to look at all options," including working with existing suppliers to boost US production.

Khan also noted that there "isn't a lot of customisation" involved in memory, suggesting off-the-shelf Chinese chips could theoretically be used in Apple devices. But US rules require American companies to obtain a license before sharing product information with CXMT and YMTC, a step that would be necessary for any customized components.

Domestic Pushback from Micron and Congress

Idaho-based Micron Technology has urged the administration to block Apple from using Chinese memory, arguing such a move could undermine domestic chip manufacturing and conflict with the government's semiconductor reshoring agenda.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=Ba0KlB-BnYk

Senators from New York, Indiana, and Idaho — states where memory chip manufacturers have announced expansion plans — wrote to Apple CEO Tim Cook in late July, urging the company not to work with Chinese memory makers.

Lutnick said the government would continue pressing Apple to move more of its supply chain to the US. "Relentlessly, more and more and more," he said. "They've built their supply chains on low-cost labour. And now they need to build a supply chain on advanced manufacturing."

Apple's Supply Chain Balancing Act

Apple has made several commitments in response to administration pressure: spending tens of billions on US-made chips for iPhones, adding a Mac Mini assembly line in Texas, securing a deal for Intel to manufacture some Apple chips, and committing to produce all iPhone and Apple Watch cover glass domestically.

But the bulk of Apple's supply chain remains in Asia. The company has been expanding iPhone assembly in India through contract manufacturing partners — a shift that serves both supply chain diversification and the growing importance of the Indian market.

Laptop makers HP and Acer have already started using CXMT memory chips in devices sold outside the US. Expanding semiconductor production can take over a year, limiting how quickly additional capacity can come online — a timeline that offers little relief for companies facing component shortages right now.

The dispute underscores the tension between the administration's push for supply chain reshoring and the practical realities of a global semiconductor market where alternatives to Chinese production are not always immediately available.
nri_angle: Apple's expanding iPhone assembly in India directly impacts the Indian manufacturing ecosystem and has implications for tech workers across the supply chain
